units.title: Unit 13 — In the living room
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use Elementary, 3rd edition, Unit 13, printed pages 32–33 (PDF pages 33–34); original or adapted practice examples.
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition)

items.section: A · Things in the living room
items.example: We spend our evenings in the living room.
items.note: A living room is a room for relaxing and spending time together. Sitting room is another common British English name.

items.section: A · Things in the living room
items.example: My dictionary is on the bookshelf.
items.note: The plural is bookshelves, not bookshelfs. A bookshelf is for storing books.

items.section: A · Things in the living room
items.example: The room has two bookshelves.
items.note: Bookshelves is the plural form of bookshelf: shelf becomes shelves.

items.section: A · Things in the living room
items.example: The light is above the table.
items.note: Light can mean the illumination or a device that produces it. Switch the light on or off.

items.section: A · Things in the living room
items.example: The window is open.
items.note: A window lets in light and can often be opened or closed.

items.section: A · Things in the living room
items.example: The curtains are blue.
items.note: The noun curtains normally occurs in the plural when referring to a pair. Open or close the curtains.

items.section: A · Things in the living room
items.example: There are books on the table.
items.note: Books is the plural of book. Books can be kept on a bookshelf or read.

items.section: A · Things in the living room
items.example: I have a lamp next to my chair.
items.note: A lamp gives light. A table lamp and a ceiling light are different kinds of light.

items.section: A · Things in the living room
items.example: There is a picture on the wall.
items.note: A picture can be a photograph, drawing or painting. A picture can hang on a wall.

items.section: A · Things in the living room
items.example: The light switch is near the door.
items.note: Use a light switch to turn a light on or off.

items.section: A · Things in the living room
items.example: The TV is opposite the sofa.
items.note: TV stands for television. Say watch TV, not watch at TV.

items.section: A · Things in the living room
items.example: My parents have an old hi-fi.
items.note: A hi-fi is an audio system for playing music, sometimes called a stereo.

items.section: A · Things in the living room
items.example: Three people can sit on our sofa.
items.note: A sofa is a long comfortable seat for two or more people. Couch is another common word.

items.section: A · Things in the living room
items.example: The table is near the window.
items.note: A table is a piece of furniture with a flat top. Compare a coffee table.

items.section: A · Things in the living room
items.example: The socket is behind the sofa.
items.note: In British English, an electrical socket is where a plug can be inserted; plug socket is also common.

items.section: A · Things in the living room
items.example: Where is the remote control?
items.note: Use a remote control to turn on the TV or change channels. Remote is a common shortened form.

items.section: A · Things in the living room
items.example: There is a rug under the coffee table.
items.note: A rug usually covers part of a floor, whereas fitted carpet may cover the whole floor.

items.section: A · Things in the living room
items.example: My phone is on the table.
items.note: Phone is a common short form of telephone. In this picture it refers to a landline phone.

items.section: A · Things in the living room
items.example: I like reading in this armchair.
items.note: An armchair is a comfortable chair with arms. We usually say sit or relax in an armchair.

items.section: A · Things in the living room
items.example: Put your cup on the coffee table.
items.note: A coffee table is a low table, often placed in front of a sofa.

items.pt: carpete; tapete que cobre o chão
items.section: A · Things in the living room
items.example: The bedroom has a grey carpet.
items.note: Carpet often covers much or all of a room floor. Compare rug, which usually covers a smaller area.

items.section: A · Things in the living room
items.example: Please sit on this chair.
items.note: You normally sit on a chair, but in an armchair.

items.section: A · Things in the living room
items.example: The furniture is comfortable.
items.note: Furniture is uncountable: say the furniture is or a piece of furniture, not furnitures are.

items.example: We watch television after dinner.
items.note: Watch is used without at: watch television, not watch at television.

items.example: My sister watches TV in the evening.
items.note: Say watch TV without a preposition. In the third person singular, use watches TV.

items.example: I listen to the radio while cooking.
items.note: Listen needs to before its object: listen to the radio, not listen the radio.

items.example: He listens to music in his room.
items.note: Say listen to music. Music is usually uncountable and has no article here.

items.example: I read a book on the sofa.
items.note: Read is written the same way in the present and past, but pronounced /riːd/ in the present and /red/ in the past.

items.example: I just want to relax tonight.
items.note: Relax means rest and stop working or worrying. Do not use relax myself or relax us in this meaning.

items.example: It gets dark early in winter.
items.note: It is getting dark describes the light changing now; it gets dark describes something that happens regularly.

items.example: Could you close the curtains?
items.note: Close the curtains means pull them together to cover the window; do not say make the curtains in this sense.

items.example: Open the curtains in the morning.
items.note: Open the curtains is the opposite of close the curtains. This is a teaching extension of the unit dialogue.

items.example: Please switch the light on.
items.note: Switch on is separable: switch the light on and switch on the light are both correct. Say switch it on.

items.example: Switch on the light, please.
items.note: Switch on is separable: switch on the light or switch the light on; with a pronoun, use switch it on.

items.example: Turn the radio off before bed.
items.note: Turn off is separable: turn the radio off, turn off the radio and turn it off are all correct.

items.example: Turn on the TV for the news.
items.note: Turn on is the opposite of turn off. Say turn on the TV or turn the TV on.

items.example: Could you pass me the remote control?
items.note: Pass + person + object is natural: pass me the remote control. You can also say pass the remote control to me.

items.example: There's a good programme on tonight.
items.note: In British English, programme is the usual spelling for a TV show. On means being broadcast.

items.example: Dad relaxes in an armchair after work.
items.note: Use in with armchair: relax in an armchair, rather than relax on an armchair.

items.example: Use the remote to change channels.
items.note: Change channels means move from one TV channel to another. A remote control can do this.

learningObjectives: Identify and name the furniture, appliances, and other objects illustrated in a living room.
Describe the location of common objects using natural combinations such as on the wall and under the table.
Use watch television, listen to music, read a book, and relax to describe activities at home.
Ask someone to close the curtains, switch on a light, turn off a radio, or pass a remote control.
Avoid common mistakes with uncountable furniture, plural bookshelves, listen to, and watch television.

units.title: Unit 14 — Jobs
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use Elementary, 3rd edition, Unit 14, printed pages 34–35 (PDF pages 35–36); original or adapted practice examples.
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition)

items.example: What is your job?
items.note: A job is a particular paid occupation or position. Work can mean employment or the activity itself, and is usually uncountable.

items.example: The doctor works at a hospital.
items.note: A doctor treats people who are ill. A doctor usually works in a hospital or surgery.

items.example: Our teacher works at a school.
items.note: A teacher helps students learn. Teachers may work in schools, colleges or universities.

items.example: The nurse is helping a patient.
items.note: A nurse cares for patients, often in a hospital. Nurses often work with doctors.

items.example: The mechanic repairs cars.
items.note: A mechanic repairs machines or vehicles, especially cars.

items.example: The secretary works in an office.
items.note: A secretary may arrange appointments, prepare documents and help with office administration.

items.example: Ask the shop assistant for help.
items.note: Shop assistant is a British English term for a person who serves customers in a shop; sales assistant is also used.

items.example: The hairdresser works in a salon.
items.note: A hairdresser cuts and styles hair. The job may be done in a hair salon or beauty salon.

items.example: My brother is an engineer.
items.note: Use an engineer, because engineer begins with a vowel sound. An engineer may design or build things.

items.example: The farmer works on a farm.
items.note: A farmer grows crops or keeps animals. The usual phrase is work on a farm.

items.example: A police officer helped me find the station.
items.note: Police officer is a gender-neutral term for a member of the police force.

items.example: The traffic warden checked the parked cars.
items.note: In British English, a traffic warden checks parking restrictions and may issue parking tickets.

items.example: The librarian helped me find a book.
items.note: A librarian helps people find and borrow books and use library services.

items.example: The bank clerk changed my money.
items.note: British English clerk is pronounced /klɑːk/; American English commonly uses /klɝːk/.

items.example: What's your job, Anna?
items.note: What is your job? asks about a person’s occupation. What do you do? is another common question.

items.example: What do you do for a living?
items.note: When discussing jobs, What do you do? asks about someone’s occupation, not their current activity.

items.example: I'm a waiter at a small restaurant.
items.note: Use a or an before a singular countable job noun: I’m a waiter; I’m an engineer.

items.example: The waiter brought our food.
items.note: A waiter serves food and drinks in a restaurant. Waitress is a traditionally female-specific alternative.

items.example: The waitress showed us to a table.
items.note: Waitress traditionally refers to a female server; waiter or server can be used when gender is not relevant.

items.example: My uncle is a taxi driver.
items.note: A taxi driver drives people to places for a fare. Driver is the general occupation word.

items.example: She has an interesting job at the museum.
items.note: An interesting job is one that attracts your attention or makes you curious. Compare boring.

items.example: The job is sometimes boring.
items.note: Something is boring if it is not interesting; a person may feel bored. The job is boring; I am bored.

items.example: Where do you work now?
items.note: Where do you work? asks for the place or organisation where a person works.

items.example: She works in a restaurant.
items.note: Use work in with a type of workplace: work in a restaurant, an office or a factory.

items.example: I work in an office near the park.
items.note: An office is a room or building where people do administrative or professional work. Say work in an office.

items.example: My father works in a factory.
items.note: Use work in a factory to describe a workplace; a factory makes or produces things.

items.example: The factory makes car parts.
items.note: A factory is a building or group of buildings where products are made.

items.example: This company makes car parts.
items.note: Car parts are pieces used to make or repair a car; parts is plural here.

items.example: I worked in a shop on Saturdays.
items.note: Work in a shop means be employed in a retail store. Shop is common British English; store is also used.

items.example: She worked at the weekends as a student.
items.note: At the weekends is common in British English. On weekends is a common alternative, particularly in American English.

items.example: She works in a beauty salon.
items.note: A beauty salon provides beauty treatments. A hairdresser may work there.

items.example: He works in a children's hospital.
items.note: Children’s is the possessive form of the irregular plural children. A children’s hospital treats children.

items.example: The writer works from home.
items.note: A writer writes books, articles or other texts. In this unit, a writer works at or from home.

items.example: I often work at home on Fridays.
items.note: Work at home focuses on the location where you work. Work from home commonly suggests working remotely.

items.example: She works from home twice a week.
items.note: Work from home commonly describes remote working, with home as the base rather than an office.

items.example: The bus driver stopped at the station.
items.note: A bus driver drives a bus. This job is the answer to a clue in Exercise 14.3.

items.example: My aunt works in a school.
items.note: Work in a school describes a place of work. Teachers and other staff may work there.

items.example: Many nurses work in hospitals.
items.note: Work in a hospital describes the workplace. Doctors and nurses often work there.

items.example: I want to work as a hairdresser.
items.note: Work as describes a job or role, while work in often describes a workplace: work as a hairdresser in a salon.

items.example: Engineers help build roads and bridges.
items.note: Build roads and bridges describes civil engineering work; the phrase gives a clue to engineer in Exercise 14.4.

items.example: Can I change money at this bank?
items.note: Change money means exchange money from one currency to another. You can change money at some banks.

learningObjectives: Identify common occupations illustrated in the unit and connect them with typical workplaces.
Ask and answer questions about occupations using What’s your job?, What do you do?, and Where do you work?
Use a or an correctly before singular job nouns and distinguish a job from work.
Describe workplaces using work in, work at home, work from home, and the related phrase work as.
Use occupational clues from the exercises to connect jobs with tasks, such as building roads or changing money.
